claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles as a function of particle size.
The thermal stability of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles decreases as particle size decreases.
The initial material consists of as-synthesized FeCuCrCoNi HEA nanoparticles.
The nanoparticles have a controlled size distribution ranging from a few nanometers to several tens of nanometers.
A progressive thermal-ramping protocol can be applied in molecular dynamics simulations.
The simulations can compare FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles across multiple particle sizes under a common thermal ramp.
Nanoparticle size determines the surface-to-volume ratio.
Nanoparticle size affects the local atomic coordination at the particle surface.
Smaller nanoparticles contain a higher proportion of surface atoms.
Surface atoms have lower coordination numbers than interior atoms.
Lower atomic coordination produces reduced thermal binding.
The greater influence of surface energy in smaller particles accelerates the onset of melting or structural transformation relative to larger particles.
The effective melting temperature or onset temperature for significant atomic disordering will decline systematically with decreasing nanoparticle size.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk material experience weaker surface effects and have a higher melting temperature.
The proposed simulation excludes oxidation, long-term environmental interactions, and extended-timescale diffusion effects.
The predicted thermal response depends on the accuracy of the selected interatomic potential and simulation parameters.
Caloric curves, mean-square displacement, and radial distribution functions can be used as indicators of melting, atomic mobility, and loss of crystalline order.
